clue.text: Farm building houses an aquatic pachyderm

definitions.text: Farm building houses an aquatic pachyderm

parts.words: Farm building houses an aquatic pachyderm
parts.note: a farm building whose name has the river horse of Africa, the hippopotamus in its short form, sitting inside it

explanation.surface: A barn on the farm turns out to be home to a hippo.
explanation.walkthrough: A shippon is a cattle shed, and the word holds HIPPO between S and N: the clue describes the answer's spelling rather than building it from separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A shippon is a dialect word for a cowshed or byre, a building on a farm.

clue.text: Like Maud when I kissed her hand

definitions.text: Like Maud when I kissed her hand

parts.words: Like Maud when I kissed her hand
parts.note: in Tennyson's poem Maud the speaker kisses her slender hand and she takes the kiss calmly

explanation.surface: A recollection of a lady's reaction to a kiss on the hand.
explanation.walkthrough: Tennyson's Maud: 'I kiss'd her slender hand, She took the kiss sedately'.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking a kiss sedately means calmly and composedly, the manner Tennyson gives Maud.

clue.text: Invest in a good seat

parts.note: the stalls are the best seats on the ground floor of a theatre

explanation.surface: Advice to put money into a theatre seat.
explanation.walkthrough: A theatre STALL is a seat on the ground floor near the stage; 'Invest' means to put someone formally into office.
explanation.definitionFit: To invest a bishop or knight is to place them formally in office, the same as setting them up in post.

clue.text: Formal skysign the flock elect to follow — to the White House?

parts.note: prim means stiffly proper and formal

parts.words: skysign the flock elect to follow
parts.note: Aries is the Ram among the signs of the zodiac, and a flock of sheep follows the ram

explanation.surface: A stiff sign in the sky shows the faithful which way to the President's residence.
explanation.walkthrough: ARIES, the Ram, is a sign in the sky, and sheep follow a ram; American primaries choose the party candidates on the way to the White House.
explanation.definitionFit: Primary elections pick each party's presidential nominee, the first stage of the road to the US presidency.

clue.text: Curious chap, that, drawing up at the next meter

definitions.text: Curious chap, that, drawing up at the next meter

parts.words: Curious chap, that, drawing up at the next meter
parts.note: a driver who noses into the next parking space is, read literally, a nose-first parker, and the phrase is also an idiom for a busybody

explanation.surface: An inquisitive man pulls in beside the next parking meter.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom for a busybody is split literally: a motorist who noses his car into the space at the next parking meter.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names a prying, inquisitive person who meddles in others' business.

clue.text: Kiss the lovely ? Sounds just the ticket !

indicators.note: the word sounds tells us the kiss and the lovely one are only heard, then respelt

parts.note: buss is an old word for a kiss, and the lovely one is the fair

explanation.surface: A suitor kisses the beautiful girl and declares it is just what was wanted.
explanation.walkthrough: BUSS (kiss) plus FAIR (the lovely) is said like BUS FARE; 'just the ticket' looks like the phrase for something perfect but is the plain sense of paying for a ticket.
explanation.definitionFit: The money paid for a ride on a bus buys exactly the passenger's ticket.

clue.text: Again first at Bisley

indicators.note: first at tells us to take the opening letters of the next word

explanation.surface: A marksman shoots again first at the Bisley range.
explanation.walkthrough: BIS is the opening of 'Bisley', England's national shooting ground; bis is the cry for an encore, meaning 'twice'.
explanation.definitionFit: Bis is Latin for twice, used to call for a repeat, a second time.

clue.text: Drink to keep elbow raised ?

definitions.meaning: a cloth support for an injured arm holds the elbow up; raising the elbow is also slang for drinking

explanation.definitionFit: A gin cocktail shares its name with a cloth support that holds up an injured arm.

clue.text: A dull turn a newspaper man referred to

indicators.note: turn tells us to reverse the word before it

parts.note: ED is short for editor, the man who runs a newspaper

explanation.surface: A tedious newspaper man takes his turn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turn' reverses DULL to LLUD; the second 'a' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: To allude to something is to mention it indirectly, to make reference to it.

clue.text: In what he requests Antony makes reservations

indicators.note: In tells us the general's first name sits inside the thing he asks for

parts.note: Mark Antony's speech begins 'Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears'
Mark is Antony's first name

explanation.surface: Mark Antony's speech contains his booking requests.
explanation.walkthrough: In Shakespeare's Julius Caesar Antony asks the crowd to 'lend me your ears', so what he requests is EARS; MARK goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: To earmark funds is to set them aside for a purpose, reserving them.

clue.text: Sacks girls of an infernal boss

parts.note: Dis is the Roman god who rules the underworld
misses are young unmarried women

explanation.surface: The devil's daughters get sacked from their jobs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'girls of an infernal boss' reads as DIS's MISSES, so DIS comes first in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To sack someone is to fire or discharge them from a job.

clue.text: Johnson did not contribute to Jerome's

definitions.text: Johnson did not contribute to Jerome's

parts.words: Johnson did not contribute to Jerome's
parts.note: Samuel Johnson wrote a series of essays under one title, and Jerome K. Jerome later edited a magazine with the same title, though Johnson wrote nothing for it

explanation.surface: A literary note that Dr Johnson never wrote for Jerome's magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: Dr Johnson's essay series The Idler (1758-60) and Jerome K. Jerome's monthly The Idler (1892 on) share a name; Johnson, long dead, could not write for the later one.
explanation.definitionFit: The title shared by Johnson's essays and Jerome's magazine is a word for a lazy person.

clue.text: What follows the flowers that bloom in the spring ?

definitions.text: What follows the flowers that bloom in the spring ?

parts.words: What follows the flowers that bloom in the spring
parts.note: a line from a Gilbert and Sullivan song in The Mikado, whose title phrase is followed by a nonsense refrain

explanation.surface: A question about what comes after spring blossoms.
explanation.walkthrough: The Mikado's song runs 'The flowers that bloom in the spring, tra la'; the surface asks about seasons, but the answer is the refrain that follows the line.
explanation.definitionFit: Tra la is a sung nonsense refrain, the words that come next in the song's opening line.

clue.text: Whom Thomson enjoyed coaching for Bisley ?

definitions.text: Whom Thomson enjoyed coaching for Bisley ?

parts.words: Whom Thomson enjoyed coaching for Bisley
parts.note: the poet James Thomson called it a delightful task to teach the youthful mind how to shoot, and Bisley is the shooting range

explanation.surface: A question about whom a coach liked training for a shooting contest.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomson's The Seasons has 'Delightful task! ... To teach the young idea how to shoot', meaning helping a child's mind grow; Bisley, in Surrey, is England's national rifle-shooting ground, so the clue reads 'shoot' as firing a gun.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase stands for a child's developing mind, the pupil a teacher brings on.

clue.text: Not forced out it, is, understood ?

definitions.meaning: not squeezed or pressed out, as juice that remains in a fruit
implied but never said aloud or stated

explanation.definitionFit: A thing implied but never stated is unspoken, and juice never squeezed out also fits.

clue.text: Last month I took a wife-it's the end !

parts.note: ult., short for ultimo, means last month in old business letters
a mate is a spouse

explanation.surface: A man recalls marrying last month and declares it the finish of his freedom.
explanation.walkthrough: ULT. (ultimo) is the old commercial abbreviation for 'last month', as in 'your letter of the 5th ult.'
explanation.definitionFit: The ultimate is the final point, the last thing beyond which nothing comes.

clue.text: Tent-dweller turned leading communist

indicators.note: turned tells us to read the tent-dweller's name back to front

parts.note: Kedar is the Biblical tribe whose tents are mentioned in Psalm 120 and the Song of Songs

explanation.surface: A nomad in a tent has become a top Bolshevik.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned' reverses KEDAR to give the name; Karl Radek was a leading Soviet communist of the 1920s.
explanation.definitionFit: Karl Radek was a prominent Bolshevik and Comintern figure, a leading man of the Communist movement.

clue.text: "Gin a body meet a body …" Or wouldn't this be a more apposite tot to offer?

definitions.text: Gin a body meet a body …" Or wouldn't this be a more apposite tot to offer

parts.words: Gin a body meet a body
parts.note: Burns's song continues 'comin' thro' the rye', and gin here means 'if', yet the solver is asked which spirit would suit better than gin

explanation.surface: A drinker suggests a better spirit to toast with than gin when meeting someone.
explanation.walkthrough: In Burns's 'Comin' Thro' the Rye', 'gin' is Scots for 'if'; reading it as the spirit, the clue asks for a more suitable drink, a spirit distilled from rye.
explanation.definitionFit: A spirit distilled from rye grain matches the field of the song's title better than gin does.

clue.text: Ernie, at your service

parts.note: ERNIE is the machine that picks Premium Bond winners, so its customers are bond holders; at your service suggests a serf

explanation.surface: A servant named Ernie introduces himself.
explanation.walkthrough: ERNIE is the British machine that draws Premium Bond prizes, whose customers hold bonds; 'at your service' points to a serf bound to a master.
explanation.definitionFit: A bondsman is a serf bound to serve, and here also a holder of government bonds.

clue.text: Go back, old thing, they look an ugly lot

indicators.note: back tells us to write the word go from right to left

parts.note: res is the Latin, an ancient tongue, for a thing

explanation.surface: Someone is told to retreat, old chap, from an unattractive crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go back' turns GO into OG; 'old thing' is RES, the Latin for 'thing', and 'old thing' in the surface sounds like a friendly address.
explanation.definitionFit: Ogres are hideous giants of folk tales, monsters famous for their ugliness.

clue.text: "A —— set with little wilful thorns" (Tennyson)

parts.note: a line from Tennyson's Maud describing a young flower before it opens, with the missing word filling the gap

explanation.surface: A quotation with a gap from a Tennyson poem.
explanation.walkthrough: Tennyson's Maud: 'A rosebud set with little wilful thorns'.
explanation.definitionFit: An unopened rose with thorns is the flower Tennyson describes in the line.

clue.text: Finnish folk laid out flat — get. brown

definitions.text: Finnish folk laid out flat — get. brown

parts.words: Finnish folk laid out flat — get. brown
parts.note: fish, the folk with fins, are split open and laid flat, then cured in smoke until they turn brown

explanation.surface: People from Finland lie stretched out and get a tan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finnish' is read as 'fin-ish', fish-like: a herring split, flattened and smoked brown has been treated this way.
explanation.definitionFit: A herring that has been split, salted and smoked turns brown, the process that makes a kipper.

clue.text: Candidate may not yet get in

definitions.meaning: someone putting themselves forward for a contest or exam
someone who has entered but has not yet been admitted or chosen

explanation.definitionFit: A competitor who has applied for a contest has entered but is not yet sure of a place.

clue.text: Man of straw?

parts.note: a man's hat woven from straw, rather than a feeble person or a scarecrow

explanation.surface: A question about a weak, insubstantial person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man of straw' suggests a weak figure, but it is a man's hat made of straw.
explanation.definitionFit: A boater is a stiff flat straw hat worn by men.

clue.text: Fire !

parts.note: the order to a gunner or a sacking from a job, both meaning to let something go or send someone away

explanation.surface: A single shouted command, as on a firing range or to a dismissed worker.
explanation.definitionFit: To fire a gun is to let it off, and to fire a worker is to dismiss them; both senses fit.

clue.text: Marble of dream

parts.note: the song 'I dreamt I dwelt in marble...' from Balfe's opera The Bohemian Girl

explanation.surface: A dream about marble.
explanation.walkthrough: Balfe's The Bohemian Girl has the aria 'I dreamt I dwelt in marble halls'.
explanation.definitionFit: The grand rooms in the song were made of marble, the large chambers of the dream.

clue.text: O that bishop !

parts.note: a cry about the cruel bishop of Mainz in legend, whose name is made from the letters of the exclamation's first two words

explanation.surface: An exasperated cry about a troublesome bishop.
explanation.walkthrough: Legend says Archbishop Hatto of Mainz burned starving peasants and was eaten by mice in his Mouse Tower; the letters of 'O that' rearrange to his name, though no word signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Hatto was the archbishop of Mainz who in legend was devoured by mice for his cruelty.

clue.text: Madam will you amble?

parts.note: the old song 'Madam, will you walk' with walk swapped for a word whose letters spell a woman's name

explanation.surface: A gentleman invites a lady out for a gentle stroll.
explanation.walkthrough: The folk song asks 'Madam, will you walk?'; 'amble' is a rearrangement of the name, and the lady addressed is the answer, though no word signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Mabel is a woman's first name, the madam being addressed.

clue.text: Briefing of worker in the Underground ?

definitions.text: Briefing of worker in the Underground ?

parts.words: Briefing of worker in the Underground
parts.note: a member of a wartime secret resistance movement, given in shortened form, rather than a London Tube employee

explanation.surface: Instructions given to someone who works on the London Tube.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Underground' suggests the London Tube, but it is the secret wartime resistance; 'Briefing' means the word for its member cut short, not an instruction session.
explanation.definitionFit: A resister in an occupied country belonged to the underground movement, and the adjective in shortened form names such a worker.

clue.text: Foreign head, British artist's rendering

definitions.meaning: an Ethiopian prince or regional chief bears this title

explanation.walkthrough: Read as R.A.'s, the second sense is 'belonging to a Royal Academician', a British artist; 'rendering' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A ras is an Ethiopian title for a prince or regional chief, a head from abroad.

clue.text: Undonnish types

parts.note: read as un-donn-ish: people who have not donned any clothes, rather than people unlike university dons

explanation.surface: People who are not scholarly or academic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Undonnish' looks like 'not like a university don', but split it as un-donned: those who have put on no clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: Naturists go about without clothes, never having put any garments on.

clue.text: "So sinks the —— in the ocean bed" (Milton)

definitions.text: "So sinks the —— in the ocean bed" (Milton)

parts.note: a line from Milton's Lycidas about the sun setting in the sea, with the missing word filling the gap

explanation.surface: A quotation with a gap from Milton's elegy Lycidas.
explanation.walkthrough: Lycidas has 'So sinks the day-star in the ocean bed': the morning sun going down into the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: The day-star is a poetic name for the sun, which seems to sink into the sea at dusk.
